seoDescription: Explore the future of Svelte with the official introduction to Svelte 5, presented by creator Rich Harris. This preview unveils Runes, a powerful new feature set designed to streamline reactivity and solve common pain points. Learn how Runes like `$state`, `$derived`, and `$effect` make your code more consistent, easily refactorable, and more performant through fine-grained reactivity. This major update simplifies state management and logic encapsulation, all while ensuring backward compatibility for a seamless upgrade.

chapters.title: Introduction to Svelte 5
chapters.description: Rich Harris introduces the Svelte 5 preview and sets the stage by discussing the strengths of the current version of Svelte.

chapters.title: Pain Point 1: The Reactive Label (`$:`)
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates the limitations of Svelte's reactive label syntax, including timing inconsistencies and difficulties with code refactoring.

chapters.title: Pain Point 2: Reusability and Custom Stores
chapters.description: This section explains how moving reactive logic into a function breaks it, forcing developers to use the more complex custom store API for encapsulation.

chapters.title: Pain Point 3: Inefficient List Reactivity
chapters.description: This chapter highlights how Svelte's current reactivity model can cause unnecessary work by invalidating an entire list when a single item within it changes.

chapters.title: The Promise of Svelte 5 and Introduction to Runes
chapters.description: Rich Harris introduces Runes as the solution to Svelte's pain points, promising a better developer experience while maintaining backward compatibility.

chapters.title: The `$state` Rune
chapters.description: This chapter introduces the `$state` rune, explaining how it creates reactive values and how it's powered by signals under the hood.

chapters.title: The `$derived` Rune
chapters.description: Learn about the `$derived` rune, which replaces the reactive label (`$:`) for creating computed values that are always in sync and easily refactorable.

chapters.title: Seamless Logic Encapsulation with Runes
chapters.description: This section demonstrates how Runes make it trivial to encapsulate reactive logic into reusable functions that can even be moved to external modules.

chapters.title: The `$effect` Rune for Side Effects
chapters.description: Discover `$effect`, a rune for running side effects that's browser-only, can replace `onMount`, and supports cleanup functions and nesting for better organization.

chapters.title: The `$props` Rune for Component APIs
chapters.description: This chapter introduces `$props`, a new rune for declaring all component props in a single, unified way using familiar destructuring syntax.

chapters.title: Conclusion and Next Steps
chapters.description: Rich Harris summarizes the benefits of Runes, thanks the community, and invites viewers to try the Svelte 5 preview and join the discussion on Discord.

summary:
## The Problem with Svelte Today

Svelte is a beloved framework, but its current design has several pain points that Svelte 5 aims to solve:

- **`$:` Reactivity:** The reactive label (`$:`) has limitations. Its value is not updated immediately, which can cause synchronization issues when logging or using the value within the same event tick. Dependency tracking is also compile-time only, making it difficult to refactor logic into separate functions.

- **Logic Encapsulation:** Reusing reactive logic is cumbersome. Extracting `let` and `$` declarations into a helper function breaks their reactivity, forcing a switch to the more verbose custom store API (`writable`, `update`, `subscribe`).

- **List Inefficiency:** When an item inside an `each` block is updated, Svelte currently invalidates the entire list. This causes expressions that depend on the list to be re-evaluated unnecessarily, leading to performance issues with large lists.

## Introducing Runes

**Runes** are special function-like symbols that provide instructions to the Svelte compiler, enabling a new, more powerful and explicit reactivity model.

> [!NOTE]
> Runes are **opt-in**. Existing Svelte 4 components will continue to work, and you can mix old and new components in the same application for an incremental, seamless upgrade.

## Core Runes Explained

### `$state`

Creates a reactive state variable. This is the foundation of reactivity in Svelte 5.

- **Usage**: `let count = $state(0);`
- **Mechanism**: Assignments like `count++` are automatically converted by the compiler into signal `set` calls, triggering fine-grained updates.

### `$derived`

Creates a computed value that reacts to changes in state variables. It's the replacement for the `$: label`.

- **Usage**: `let doubled = $derived(count * 2);`
- **Benefits**: It is lazily evaluated but always stays in sync. It supports runtime dependency tracking, so refactoring logic into functions works as expected.

### `$effect`

Runs side effects in response to state changes. It's the replacement for `$: { ... }` blocks.

- **Usage**: `$effect(() => { console.log('Count is', count); });`
- **Key Features**:
  - Runs only in the browser, after the DOM has been updated.
  - A cleanup function can be returned, which runs before the next effect execution or on unmount.
  - Can be nested for better code organization.

> [!TIP]
> Because `$effect` runs after mount, it can often replace the `onMount` lifecycle function.

### `$props`

Provides a modern, unified API for declaring component props.

- **Usage**: `let { name, class: className, ...rest } = $props();`
- **Benefits**: Replaces `export let`, handles default values and reserved keywords elegantly, and consolidates access to `$restProps` via standard destructuring.

## Key Benefits of Svelte 5

- **Consistency**: JavaScript code behaves the same inside and outside of `.svelte` files, eliminating the "magical" context-aware behavior.
- **Simplicity**: Fewer core concepts to learn. Runes replace special syntax (`$:`, `export let`) and reduce the need for stores and lifecycle functions.
- **Refactorability**: Reactive logic is easily astracted into reusable functions and modules without changing its behavior.
- **Performance**: Fine-grained reactivity powered by signals means only the parts of your app that truly need to update will do so.

## Next Steps

- **Try it out**: Visit the interactive playground at [svelte5preview.vercel.app](https://svelte5preview.vercel.app).
- **Join the community**: Ask questions and provide feedback in the `svelte-5-runes` channel on the official Svelte Discord server.
transcription:
## Introduction to Svelte 5

All right friends, gather 'round and let's talk about Svelte 5. A lot of you know that we've been hard at work on the next version of Svelte for a while now, and in this video I'm going to share a preview of some of the new stuff and hopefully get you all as excited about it as we are.

## Pain Point 1: The Reactive Label (`$:`)

Before we do that, I want to talk about Svelte today. We like Svelte, we're proud of Svelte and all of the love that it gets in developer surveys and so on. We think it's the best way to build most web apps.

But there are some undeniable pain points that you've probably encountered and which are difficult to fix with Svelte's current design. Let's look at a simple component that we might write today. We're declaring a count variable and using its value inside our template. Every time we update its value inside the event handler, the page automatically updates. Very cool, very easy to learn because there's no API, we're just using the language.

If I want to add a derived value, I can do that with `$: doubled = count * 2`, and that will be updated whenever count changes. There's a little gotcha here though, because Svelte doesn't want to run this code until it's sure that there are no other changes to take account of. It won't recalculate `doubled` until right before the DOM is updated. So if, for example, you log the values inside the increment function, you'll see that they get out of sync.

Another gotcha is that the dependency tracking happens at compile time. What I mean by that is that the compiler looks at this expression on the right, it's `count * 2`, and understands that the value of `doubled` is dependent on the value of `count`. But what if we refactor our code by having a `doubleCount` function? The compiler can no longer see the dependency, which means that `doubled` will never be updated. This makes it a little hard to refactor code out of `$: label` statements, which means that they tend to attract complexity.

## Pain Point 2: Reusability and Custom Stores

Now, let's imagine that we want to encapsulate this logic so that it can be reused, perhaps when I have multiple counters on the page. I might try wrapping it in a `createCounter` function like this, but this completely changes the meaning of the code. It no longer behaves the same way because it's no longer at the top level of the component. The `let` no longer becomes magically reactive, and this `$: label` has no special meaning at all. This is just an assignment to an undeclared variable.

So at this point, we have to use a completely different mechanism: we have to use a custom store. First, we import `writable` from `svelte/store`, and then we create a writable store inside `createCounter` so that we can steal its `subscribe` and `update` functions. If an object has a `subscribe` method, then it's a store, so we can return that from our function along with `increment`. But `increment` can't just assign directly to `count` anymore; we need to use this `update` function with a callback that produces a new value from the old value. And I'm not even going to get into how you would implement `doubled` here.

Once we've done all that, we can create a counter object, update the event handler, and reference the store value by prefixing it with a dollar sign. And now our counter works again in a reusable form. Now, I'm speed-running large chunks of the Svelte tutorial here, and I'm zeroing in on problematic things, but I think you get the idea. There is room for improvement.

## Pain Point 3: Inefficient List Reactivity

Let's take another example: a to-do list. In this demo, we have an `each` block with some bindings. When we toggle these checkboxes, we recalculate this `remaining todos` expression down here. I've added some logging so that we can see when it gets called. Notice that when I change the text of a to-do, it recalculates that remaining count, and you can see the count tick up in the console in the bottom right.

The way that this all works is that when you update a value inside an `each` block, Svelte will jump through some hoops to figure out what underlying piece of state may have changed as a result. And in this case, it can clearly see that each to-do is a member of the `todos` list, meaning any changes that happen inside the `each` block will invalidate the entire `todos` list. As a result, this `remaining todos` expression is re-evaluated.

The trouble is that when `todos` is invalidated, Svelte needs to check this entire list. It's able to do that pretty fast, but you can imagine that if this list was very long, that would cause a lot of unnecessary work.

## The Promise of Svelte 5 and Introduction to Runes

Svelte 5 fixes all this. It's going to make your app smaller, faster, easier to understand, easier to refactor, more consistent, all around better. And even though I'm going to be showing you some new stuff, the framework is actually going to get easier to learn because a number of the things that you have to understand today will no longer be necessary in the new world.

Now that sounds like a lot of change, and so I want to reassure you that what I'm about to show you is opt-in. Your existing components will continue to work, and you can mix and match the new mode with the old mode. We are totally committed to this being a seamless upgrade that you can apply incrementally.

So without further ado, it brings me great pleasure to introduce Runes. A rune is a letter or mark used as a mystical or magic symbol. In Svelte, runes are function-like symbols that provide instructions to the Svelte compiler.

## The `$state` Rune

The first rune we're going to learn is `state`. Let's go back to our counter example—not our *counter example*, our counter example, two words. The first thing I'm going to do is use the `state` rune to mark `count` as a reactive value.

At first you might look at that and think, but why? Maybe you're thinking of the meme. Maybe you're even blowing up. "Oh, damn you! God damn you all to hell!"

Bear with me, I promise this will all make sense very soon. You can see that everything just works like before. All we need to do to update this value is assign to it. Under the hood, Svelte is using something called signals to make this work. `count` is turned into a source signal. The assignment is turned into a `set` call. And we have something down here called a render effect that updates the DOM. When this function runs, we call this `get` function. The `count` source knows that it should notify that render effect whenever its value changes.

## The `$derived` Rune

If I try and put `doubled` back in using the `$: label`, it's going to yell at me because we're now in runes mode by virtue of the fact that we're using the `state` rune. So instead of that, we're going to learn the next rune: `derived`. In runes mode, we say `let doubled = $derived(count * 2)`.

Now, `derived` behaves a little bit differently to the `$: label`. Remember before how the values got out of sync? That no longer happens. The value is still recalculated lazily, but it's recalculated when we need it, so it stays in sync. You'll also recall if we refactored this into a function, it would break. That no longer happens because we're tracking dependencies when the expression is evaluated.

## Seamless Logic Encapsulation with Runes

A few minutes ago when we tried to encapsulate this logic into a reusable function, it got a bit ugly. With runes it is much, much simpler. I can just wrap this up inside a `createCounter` function and the runes will continue to work. Notice that I'm using a `get` property here. That's because if I just returned `count`, it'll be whatever the value was at the time the function was called. And we want `counter.count` to always refer to the current value.

What's really cool about this is I can move it into an external module and it still works. There's no code changes necessary. You no longer have this magical technicolor experience inside your Svelte components but a lousy black and white one everywhere else. We've Svelted all over your code base.

## The `$effect` Rune for Side Effects

Another example: here we've got a fun little canvas painting app. Inside the component, we have an `onMount` which runs some code when the component is mounted to the DOM. Below that, we have a reactive statement using the `$: label` syntax. The first thing we need to do is check that our canvas context has been created.

If we opt into runes mode by turning this `mouse` value into reactive state, we'll get a compiler error telling us that we can't use the `$: label` and should use `derived` or `effect` instead. So let's learn about the `effect` rune. `effect` is what you use when you want something to happen in response to something changing. I'm going to paste this code into our effect, and I'm going to delete the outer `if context` code. The reason I can do that is effects only ever run in the browser after the DOM has been updated, so `context` is guaranteed to have been created in `onMount`. In fact, if we look at the JavaScript output and switch it into SSR mode, we can see that the effect has been completely removed from the output. The `onMount` is still there, though.

Now, if you're using SvelteKit or you've managed to set up your build tooling correctly, then that will get removed later on, but maybe we don't need it here either. It turns out that you can use effects instead of `onMount` as well. Now we can delete the import and see that it's all been removed from our SSR output and everything continues to work.

We can also return functions from our effects. These functions will be called whenever the effect refires, and also when the component is unmounted. We can also nest effects, so we can put this update effect inside the initialization effect, and now we can avoid cluttering up the top level scope.

All in all, it just allows you to encapsulate your code a little bit more logically than you could in the old world.

## The `$props` Rune for Component APIs

There's one last rune to show you, and that's the `props` rune. Today in Svelte, if you want to declare a prop, then use `export let` to define the prop and then optionally provide a default value. If no default value is provided, it means the prop is required. If a prop is a reserved word like `catch`, then we can't declare it locally, so we have to create the prop in two stages. First we declare a local alias, and then we export the alias to the outside world. If we want to get all of the other props that weren't explicitly declared, we need to use this `$$restProps` thing. Finally, we can also export functions. This isn't a prop, it's actually a method on the component. Over in `App.svelte`, we have a reference to this child component provided by the `bind:this` binding and we can call its methods from outside.

If we instead use the `props` rune, we can declare all our props in one go using familiar destructuring syntax. And I can't show you this in the playground because we don't have TypeScript rigged up, but you can also use a type argument here to define the shape of your props.

All in all, I think this is a pretty substantial upgrade.

## Conclusion and Next Steps

So that's a very quick introduction to Svelte 5. There's a lot more cool stuff that doesn't fit into a short video, but hopefully this has piqued your interest. With Runes, Svelte becomes a much simpler framework. You don't need to understand the special `let` behavior, you don't need to understand the `$: label`, you don't need to understand how `export` works, you don't need to switch mental modes between Svelte and non-Svelte JavaScript. You probably won't need to use stores or lifecycle functions, and so when people come to our community in future, they're going to have a much easier time getting comfortable.

I think if anything, I'm more excited about what this means for people who are already maintaining sizable Svelte codebases. We've spent a lot of time converting existing apps and libraries to see how it feels, and it really does feel good.

You can't install it yet, we don't have a release date, but the good news is that you can visit this playground right now. Just go to svelte5preview.vercel.app. We have docs, we have an FAQ, and a link to the Discord server so that you can come and ask your Runes questions in the Svelte 5 Runes channel.

And I want to take a moment to acknowledge the hard work done by the team on this. This wasn't easy, it took a lot, but hopefully you'll agree that it's going to be worth it. I want to thank the Svelte ambassadors who have given us a ton of great feedback that's helped us refine the design. I want to thank all of the other framework communities whose research we're very much building on top of... good luck catching us now! And I want to thank you for watching. See you in Discord.
